decisionMemo.businessProblem: A boutique practice depends entirely on one owner-operator who holds all client relationships and pricing knowledge; the owner wants to reduce the single point of failure.

rootCauseDiagnosis.description: Key-person dependency: critical knowledge / relationships concentrated in one person
rootCauseDiagnosis.mechanismDescription: Critical system knowledge, client relationships, or revenue are concentrated in a single undocumented person with no succession — a single point of failure that survives any program-level fix.
alternativeExplanations: A general staffing constraint rather than a single-person dependency
A documented role that can be back-filled without knowledge loss
missingEvidenceFor: The exact knowledge and relationships held only by that person
Cross-training / succession readiness of the next-best resource

intervention.title: Map key-person dependencies and begin knowledge capture and cross-training
intervention.objective: Reduce the key-person point of failure by capturing knowledge before new work
intervention.rationale: Key-person dependency mapping with knowledge capture and cross-training is low-cost and reversible, reducing the key-person concentration before new engagements.
intervention.whyThisNow: Critical knowledge and relationships concentrate in one person; capture and cross-training must precede new work

steps.title: Map the key-person dependencies
steps.description: Map the dependencies and the concentration of knowledge, relationships, and revenue on that person.
steps.successCriteria: Key-person dependencies and revenue concentration mapped

steps.title: Stand up knowledge capture and cross-training
steps.description: Document the undocumented knowledge and cross-train a second qualified resource to remove the point of failure.
steps.successCriteria: Knowledge-capture and cross-training plan underway with a second qualified resource

failureRisks: The key person may resist documentation or transfer
intervention.fallbackPlan: Capture the highest-risk knowledge and relationships first while a second resource is recruited

factors.rationale: Expected revenue impact: MINOR. Urgency: HIGH
Duration: 7 days. Team capacity: LOW. Cost: LOW
Failure risks: 1. Fallback plan available: Yes
Cost band: LOW vs Expected impact: MINOR

recommendedInterventions.sequencingReason: Quick implementation builds momentum and shows progress

scenarios.name: Aggressive Recovery (Best Case)
scenarios.description: Execute all interventions in optimal sequence with full team commitment
assumptions: Team capacity fully available (no other initiatives)
Client budget approved for all recommended interventions
No external market shocks during implementation
scenarios.expectedOutcome: Revenue recovery within 90 days, competitive positioning restored
risks: Cascading failures if one intervention stumbles

scenarios.name: Staged Implementation (Recommended)
scenarios.description: Execute top 3 prioritized interventions sequentially, measure, then decide on next wave
assumptions: Top 3 interventions address critical path to revenue recovery
Team capacity for 1-2 major initiatives at a time
Monthly review gates to assess progress and adjust
scenarios.expectedOutcome: Measurable improvement in 60 days, foundation for growth set
risks: Slower overall recovery than aggressive path
Competitors may advance while we execute gradually

limitations: Evidence gaps limit precision: Critical gap: No evidence on Customer Retention; Weak evidence on Operational Efficiency - diagnosis confidence limited; Critical gap: No evidence on Quality Delivery
Evidence coverage is insufficient across business dimensions. Deeper investigation recommended before diagnosis finalization.
nextReviewTriggers: After first intervention completion: validate assumptions, collect outcome data
Monthly: Track KPIs (repeat customer rate, turnaround time, complaint count)
If revenue does not improve by 20% within 60 days: pivot to alternative diagnosis
If team capacity exhausted: pause non-critical interventions
If external market changes significantly: reassess competitive positioning
